{{short description|NASA Kepler planet discovery mission principal investigator}}
[[File:William Borucki NASA.jpg|thumb|William J. Borucki (date unknown).]]
'''William J. (Bill) Borucki''' (born 1939) is a [[space scientist]] who worked at the [[NASA]] [[Ames Research Center]].<ref name=kepler.nasa.gov-1>{{cite web | url=http://kepler.nasa.gov/Mission/team/williamBorucki/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100528002532/http://kepler.nasa.gov/Mission/team/williamBorucki/ | url-status=dead | archive-date=May 28, 2010 | title=Kepler: William Borucki | publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration | work=Kepler: A Search for Habitable Planets | date=December 31, 2009 | access-date=January 7, 2013}}</ref> Upon joining NASA in 1962, Borucki joined the group conducting research on the heat shield for [[Apollo program]] spacecraft.<ref name=kepler.nasa.gov-1 /> He later turned his attention to the optical efficiency of lightning strikes in the atmospheres of planets, investigating the propensity that these lightning strikes could create molecules that would later become the precursors for life.<ref name=nasa-ames-1>{{cite press release | url=http://www.nasa.gov/centers/ames/news/releases/2004/borucki/borucki.html | title=William J. Borucki | publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration | date=March 29, 2008 | access-date=January 7, 2013 | editor=Jonas Dino | archive-date=June 22, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170622092054/https://www.nasa.gov/centers/ames/news/releases/2004/borucki/borucki.html | url-status=dead }}</ref> Subsequently, Borucki's attention turned to [[extrasolar planet]]s and their detection, particularly through the [[transit method]].<ref name=nasa-ames-1 /> In light of this work, Borucki was named the principal investigator for NASA's [[Kepler space telescope]] mission, launched on March 7, 2009<ref name=kepler.nasa.gov-1 /> and dedicated to a transit-based search for habitable planets.<ref name=kepler.nasa.gov-1 /> In 2013, Borucki was awarded the United States [[National Academy of Sciences]]'s [[Henry Draper Medal]] for his work with Kepler. In 2015 he received the [[Shaw Prize]] in Astronomy.<ref name="Shaw Prize">{{cite web|title=Announcement and Citation: The Shaw Prize in Astronomy 2015|url=http://www.shawprize.org/en/shaw.php?tmp=3&twoid=98&threeid=243&fourid=434|website=The Shaw Prize|access-date=2 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150702094719/http://www.shawprize.org/en/shaw.php?tmp=3&twoid=98&threeid=243&fourid=434|url-status=dead|archive-date=2 July 2015}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
Born in [[Chicago]] in 1939, Borucki grew up in [[Delavan, Wisconsin|Delavan]], [[Wisconsin]].<ref name="Air & Space">{{cite web|last1=Lawler|first1=Andrew|title=Bill Borucki's Planet Search|url=http://www.airspacemag.com/space/bill-boruckis-planet-search-4545405/?no-ist|website=Air & Space Magazine|publisher=[[Smithsonian Institution]]|access-date=1 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150702154423/http://www.airspacemag.com/space/bill-boruckis-planet-search-4545405/?no-ist|url-status=live|archive-date=2 July 2015}}</ref> He studied [[physics]] at the [[University of Wisconsin, Madison]], earning a master's degree in the subject 1962.<ref name=nasa-ames-1 /> Following this, Borucki joined the Hypersonic Free Flight team conducting research on design for Apollo program heat shield,<ref name=nasa-ames-1 /> that was designed to protect the spacecraft and their occupants from being destroyed by the heat of re-entry into the atmosphere. After his work for Apollo, Borucki studied [[meteorology]] at [[San Jose State University]], earning a master's degree in 1982.<ref name="NASA Kepler">{{cite web|title=William Borucki, principal investigator for NASA's Kepler mission|url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/kepler/team/william_borucki.html|website=NASA|access-date=1 July 2015|archive-date=2 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150702180500/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/kepler/team/william_borucki.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> That year, Borucki began studies at NASA into the nature of lightning, using satellites equipped with instrumentation he helped design in order to discover what fraction of the energy in this lightning went into the production of prebiotic molecules.<ref name=nasa-ames-1 /> As a part of this research, Borucki conducted analysis based on observations from [[space probe]]s in order to find the frequency of lightning on other planets within the Solar System.<ref name=nasa-ames-1 />

[[File:Telescope-KeplerSpacecraft-20130103-717260main pia11824-full.jpg|left|thumb|300px|The effort to launch Kepler was spearheaded by Borucki, who is now its principal investigator.<ref name=skyandtelescope />]]By 1984, Borucki's attention had turned to the search for extrasolar planets by use of the transit method,<ref name=nasa-ames-1 /> which involves observing the periodic dimming of the star in order to detect the signature of a planet blocking some of its light as it passes in front.<ref name=nasa-kepler-1>{{cite web | url=http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/kepler/multimedia/images/kepler-transit-graph.html | title=The Transit Method of Detecting Extrasolar Planets | publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration | date=November 12, 2008 | access-date=January 11, 2013 | editor=Alexander Van Dijk | archive-date=September 8, 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180908060002/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/kepler/multimedia/images/kepler-transit-graph.html | url-status=dead }}</ref> In that year and subsequently in 1988, Borucki organized workshops of scientists in order to determine the best methods for achieving transit-based detections of exoplanets, and also worked closely with the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] to develop photometers that could achieve the sensitivity desired.<ref name=nasa-ames-1 /> At the [[Lick Observatory]], Borucki demonstrated the techniques required for extrasolar planet detection by the transit method, and later constructed a ground-based proof-of-concept for a space telescope designed to hunt for planets.<ref name=nasa-ames-1 />

Until his retirement in July 2015,<ref name="NASA retirement" /> Borucki was the chief investigator for the Kepler space telescope, designed to hunt for exoplanets with the transit method. The telescope has detected 3253 confirmed planets and thousands of likely planet candidates as of December 6, 2022.<ref name=kepler.nasa.gov-2>{{cite web | url=http://kepler.nasa.gov | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040315035540/http://www.kepler.nasa.gov/ | url-status=dead | archive-date=March 15, 2004 | title=Kepler: A Search for Habitable Planets | publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration | date=January 9, 2013 | access-date=January 11, 2013}}</ref> For his work, he has received the NASA Outstanding Leadership Award, the ''[[Popular Mechanics]]'' Breakthrough Award in 2009, and the NASA Systems Engineering Excellence Award in 2010, and the Lancelot M. Berkeley Prize for Meritorious Work in Astronomy in 2011.<ref name=smc-it>{{cite web | url=http://www.smc-it.org/bios/William-Borucki.html | title=Fourth IEEE International Conference on Space Mission Challenges for Information Technology: Keynote Presentation | publisher=Space Mission Challenges for Information Technology | work=Fourth IEEE Conference on Space Mission Challenges for Information Technology | year=2009 | access-date=January 11, 2013}}</ref> He received the 2013 Henry Draper Medal from the United States National Academy of Sciences<ref name=skyandtelescope>{{cite news | url=http://www.skyandtelescope.com/news/Kepler-Zeroes-in-on-Alien-Earths-186015912.html | title=Kepler Zeroes in on Alien Earths | work=Sky and Telescope | date=January 8, 2013 | agency=Sky and Telescope | access-date=January 11, 2013 | author=Young, Monica}}</ref> "For his founding concept, unflagging advocacy, and visionary leadership during the development of NASA's Kepler mission, which has uncovered myriad planets and solar systems with unforeseen and surprising properties."<ref name=henrydrapermedal-1>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/about-nas/awards/henry-draper-medal.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130126003930/http://www.nasonline.org/about-nas/awards/henry-draper-medal.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 26, 2013|title=Henry Draper Medal|publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]]|access-date=2011-05-27}}</ref> and the 2015 Shaw Prize in Astronomy for "his conceiving and leading the Kepler mission, which greatly advanced knowledge of both extrasolar planetary systems and stellar interiors."<ref name="Shaw Prize" />  In 2016, he was named as a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref name="aaas">{{citation|title=2016 AAAS Fellows approved by the AAAS Council| journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] | volume=354|issue=6315|pages=981–984|doi=10.1126/science.354.6315.981|date=25 November 2016| pmid=27885000 | bibcode=2016Sci...354..981. |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Personal life==
William Borucki married the former Josephine Julia Joyce in 1963.  They met while both were students at the University of Wisconsin in Madison, Wisconsin.  They have three daughters; Virginia (Joy), Monica, and Stella, five grandchildren; Georgia, Jack, Sydney, Kira, and Madeline, and two step grandchildren; Carina and Marcus (through Stella).
